text:
**Short answer:** A 1,000 Wh unit can keep a typical full-size fridge running for most of a day. A 2,000 Wh unit covers about a day and a half. Either way, the station also needs enough surge output to start the compressor.

**Three things to check**

1. **Continuous watts:** The fridge usually runs at about 100–250 W while the compressor is on, so most 1,000 W-class stations handle this easily ([3](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
2. **Surge watts:** The compressor start can spike to roughly 1,200–2,400 W. A station whose surge rating is lower will trip at the first start, however much battery it has ([3](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [5](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
3. **Watt-hours:** The compressor runs only about a third of the time, so daily energy is much lower than the label wattage suggests. One example: an 18 cu ft ENERGY STAR top-freezer uses 362 kWh/year, about 41 W average, or roughly 1,000 Wh per day. Adding inverter losses and headroom brings the requirement to about 1,400 Wh per day ([5](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).

**Runtime by capacity** (estimates vary with assumptions)

| Capacity | Approximate runtime | Source |
|---|---|---|
| ~1,000 Wh | ~17 hours to most of a day | [4](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/), [3](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) |
| ~2,000 Wh | ~1.4 days (or ~33 hours under different assumptions) | [5](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator), [4](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) |

For a full 24 hours, BlackBox recommends about 1,600–2,000 Wh ([3](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). Keeping the door shut helps a lot. The USDA says food is unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F with the door closed ([4](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).

**Options from my search results**

- **BLUETTI AC200L** (2,048 Wh, 2,400 W continuous, 3,600 W surge, pure sine wave, expandable up to 8 kWh): [Dealectric listing](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l). The listing shows $899 (list $1,599), with a code AFF5OFF for about $44.95 off, tested on 2026-10-21. It's an affiliate page, and prices change, so confirm at checkout. It weighs 28 kg.
- **Anker SOLIX S2000** (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W rated, 3,000 W peak, pure sine wave): listed at $699.99 after coupon in [Anker's own guide](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator). That is a manufacturer source, so weigh its claims accordingly.
- **BLUETTI AC180** (about 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W AC, 2,700 W peak, $399–699 range): BlackBox's top pick, with a [guide here](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage). My results don't include a direct product link, so search BLUETTI's site or Amazon for it.

**Recommendation:** For most households, a 2,000 Wh-class unit with at least 1,500 W continuous and 2,400 W surge gives comfortable margin for a day-plus outage. If budget is tight, a 1,000 Wh unit covers most of a day.

**Before you buy**

- Check your fridge's energy label. Annual kWh ÷ 8,760 × 1,000 gives its average watts ([5](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
- Check the fridge's manual or the DOE Refrigerator and Freezer Energy Rating Search Tool for model-specific figures ([2](https://www.itechguides.com/how-to-size-a-portable-power-station-for-a-refrigerator-and-essential-devices/)).
- Choose a pure sine wave inverter, since a fridge compressor is fussy about waveform ([3](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
- Estimates differ by source because they use different surge and duty-cycle assumptions. Treat the runtimes as ballpark figures.
